summary: Flies piloted eVTOL and powered-lift air taxis (Joby, Archer, Beta, EHang-style operations) on short urban routes between vertiports under emerging rules such as the FAA powered-lift SFAR (14 CFR Part 194), EASA's VTOL framework and FAA Engineering Brief 105A for vertiports, and later may supervise multiple autonomous aircraft. AI helps most with route and energy-reserve planning, briefing prep, studying fast-changing regulations and type-specific systems, debriefs and safety reports, and passenger communication, while the pilot keeps full command authority.

prompts.title: Pre-flight route and energy briefing
prompts.task: Build a structured pre-departure brief for an urban eVTOL sector.
prompts.prompt: You are a briefing assistant for a commercial eVTOL pilot flying [AIRCRAFT TYPE] from [DEPARTURE VERTIPORT] to [ARRIVAL VERTIPORT]. Using the data I paste below (METAR/TAF, winds aloft, NOTAMs/TFRs, planned route, payload, battery state of charge and the operator's energy reserve policy), produce a one-page brief with: 1) weather and wind hazards relevant to low-altitude urban flight (gusts, building-induced turbulence, density altitude); 2) relevant NOTAMs and TFRs; 3) an energy plan comparing expected consumption plus required reserve against available charge, with diversion options; 4) go/no-go flags. Mark any number you estimated rather than read from my data. Data: [PASTE DATA]
prompts.caution: Advisory only; verify against the operator's approved flight planning tools, the AFM and official weather/NOTAM sources. The PIC makes the go/no-go decision.

prompts.title: Powered-lift regulation study guide
prompts.task: Learn the current certification and operating rules for powered-lift pilots.
prompts.prompt: Act as a ground-school instructor. I am a [CURRENT CERTIFICATES, e.g. commercial helicopter / ATP airplane] pilot moving to powered-lift operations in [COUNTRY/REGULATOR]. Explain the current path to a powered-lift rating and type rating, citing the actual rules (e.g. FAA SFAR Part 194 and related Parts 61/91/135 provisions, or EASA's VTOL operations rules), including training, experience, simulator credit and instructor requirements. Present it as: a summary table, a step-by-step plan for my background, and 10 self-quiz questions with answers. Clearly flag anything that is proposed, recently changed, or that you are uncertain about, and list which official documents I should read to confirm.
prompts.caution: Rules for powered-lift are new and changing; confirm every requirement against the current regulation text and your operator's training program.

prompts.title: Abnormal procedure drill builder
prompts.task: Turn operator checklists into scenario drills for recurrent practice.
prompts.prompt: You are a training captain for [AIRCRAFT TYPE] eVTOL operations. Based only on the operator procedures I paste below, create [NUMBER] scenario-based drills for abnormal and emergency situations such as [e.g. loss of one or more lift motors, battery thermal warning, flight control degradation, lost C2/datalink, vertiport pad blocked on short final]. For each drill give: the setup and phase of flight, cues the pilot would see, the expected actions in order (quoting my procedures), key decision points, and debrief questions. Do not invent procedures; if my text does not cover a situation, say so and list it as a gap to raise with the training department. Procedures: [PASTE PROCEDURES]
prompts.caution: For study and simulator prep only; the approved AFM/QRH always takes precedence.

prompts.title: Post-flight debrief and safety report
prompts.task: Draft a factual safety report after an event or anomaly.
prompts.prompt: Help me write a safety report for my operator's SMS (and, if applicable, a draft for NASA ASRS or [OTHER REPORTING SYSTEM]). Event notes: [DATE, ROUTE, AIRCRAFT, PHASE OF FLIGHT, WHAT HAPPENED, ATC/VERTIPORT COMMS, WEATHER, CREW ACTIONS, OUTCOME]. Produce: a neutral chronological narrative, contributing factors grouped as human / aircraft / environment / organizational (e.g. using a HFACS-style lens), immediate actions taken, and suggested corrective actions. Keep the language factual and non-speculative, mark assumptions, and list questions I should answer before submitting. Remove passenger personal data.
prompts.caution: Check your operator's reporting deadlines and NTSB/authority immediate-notification rules (e.g. 49 CFR 830) separately; do not paste data your company policy forbids sharing.

prompts.title: Battery and performance trend analysis
prompts.task: Spot patterns in energy use and battery data across many sectors.
prompts.prompt: You are a data analyst supporting an eVTOL pilot. Below is a CSV export of my recent sectors with columns [e.g. date, route, payload, OAT, wind, takeoff SOC, landing SOC, cruise time, hover time, max cell temp]. Analyze: energy consumed per sector vs. payload, wind and temperature; outliers where landing state of charge was closer to the reserve minimum than usual; any upward trend in hover time or cell temperature that could matter for planning. Output a short findings list, a table of flagged sectors, and questions to raise with maintenance or flight ops. Explain your method and do not overstate conclusions from small samples. Data: [PASTE CSV]
prompts.caution: Pilot-side observations only; battery health and airworthiness determinations belong to maintenance and the manufacturer.

prompts.title: Passenger briefing and delay messaging
prompts.task: Write clear passenger safety briefings and disruption announcements.
prompts.prompt: Write passenger communications for a [NUMBER]-seat air taxi on the [ROUTE] service. Produce: 1) a 60-second spoken safety briefing covering seatbelts, headsets, doors, emergency exits and what to expect during vertical takeoff and transition, consistent with these required items from our operations manual: [PASTE REQUIRED ITEMS]; 2) three short announcements for a weather hold, a diversion to [ALTERNATE VERTIPORT], and a battery-charging delay. Tone: calm, plain English, reading level about grade 8, no promises about times we cannot keep. Also give a [SECOND LANGUAGE] version of the safety briefing.
prompts.caution: The approved operations manual's required briefing content governs; have translations checked by a fluent speaker.

prompts.title: Community noise and route explainer
prompts.task: Prepare a pilot's talking points for a community meeting about air taxi routes.
prompts.prompt: I am a line pilot asked to speak at a [CITY] community meeting about a proposed air taxi route over [NEIGHBORHOODS] to a vertiport at [LOCATION]. Using the facts I provide (route altitudes, flight frequency, published noise data from the manufacturer, curfew hours, safety record so far): [PASTE FACTS], draft 5-minute talking points and an FAQ of 10 likely resident questions with honest answers on noise, privacy, safety, emergency landing options and who regulates what (FAA/local authorities). Distinguish clearly between facts I supplied, general industry information, and open questions still being decided. Avoid marketing language.
prompts.caution: Get public statements approved by your operator's communications and legal teams before speaking.

prompts.title: Future autonomy and multi-aircraft supervision prep
prompts.task: Learn what supervising remotely piloted or autonomous air taxis would involve.
prompts.prompt: Act as a career mentor for an urban air mobility pilot preparing for a possible shift from onboard piloting to supervising [NUMBER] autonomous or remotely piloted aircraft from a ground station (as companies such as Wisk and EHang are pursuing). Explain: how today's analogues work (e.g. FAA BVLOS rulemaking under proposed Part 108, UTM/UAM concepts of operations, EHang's operations in China), which human-factors risks matter most (automation complacency, mode confusion, alert overload, handoffs), and what skills and certifications I should build over the next [TIMEFRAME]. Output a 12-month learning plan with resources. Clearly separate what exists today from what is proposed or speculative.
prompts.caution: This area is largely unregulated or in rulemaking; treat forecasts as uncertain and verify the current status of any proposal.
